posts.title: The Net will be Split
posts.excerpt: Dario Amodei's latest essay drops a throwaway line about a botnet taking over the internet. It echoes a hunch I have had for months: traffic is already splitting into a botnet and a peoplenet, and the fallout lands on privacy and advertising, not only on security.
content: I found myself reading Dario Amodei's latest essay this week, and as with most Dario essays, it covers a lot of the complexity related to figuring out this whole AI thing. Bioterrorism, model misalignment and similar issues are relevant, but a hunch of mine from 10 months ago got echoed by Dario in this throwaway sentence that I could not help but recognise.

Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it's my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails.

A botnet is a logical collection of Internet-connected devices, such as computers, smartphones or Internet of things (IoT) devices whose security has been breached and control ceded to a third party (In this context, AI agents).
For the first time ever, bot traffic has surpassed human traffic over the internet.

Specifically, more than half the web requests made over the Internet are now done by automated systems rather than humans, I would argue likely due to the integration of web search into most AI model providers.

To understand what taking over the internet would even mean, it helps to know that there is no single internet to take. What we call the internet is tens of thousands of independently run networks that have agreed to carry each other's traffic, held together by a routing protocol that mostly assumes everyone is telling the truth about where they can deliver packets. There is no big red button, and no list of everyone who is allowed on. Because the network layer does not police access, access control lives at the edges, in the servers that decide whether to answer a given request. For most of the web's life those decisions rested on rather thin evidence. A server could look at your IP address, which says roughly where a request came from but nothing about who sent it. It could read the User-Agent header, a line of text the requester writes about itself and can therefore write anything into. And it could publish robots.txt, a file that tells crawlers which paths to leave alone, which has never been a lock so much as a note on the door.
Every one of those signals is a claim rather than a proof.

The other thing that changed is that most websites no longer answer their own requests. A content delivery network (CDN) sits in front of the origin server, keeping cached copies of pages in data centres near the people asking for them, so a reader in Tokyo is served from Tokyo rather than waiting on a machine in Virginia. CDNs took this on for speed and for absorbing DDoS attacks, but the consequence is that every request to a site passes through one intermediary first.
That intermediary is where the decision to allow or refuse gets made, and where the split between the bots and the humans can occur.

I had a hunch 10 months ago that due to AI agents increasingly becoming more capable and autonomous we will have two mass communication platforms, one for them, and one for us. Given that the bot traffic has surpassed human traffic for the first time ever this year, and that Cloudflare has published stricter delineations and protocols and unique forms of identifying humans vs agents, I think we are already headed there.
Now there is a version of this that is more benign, such as hardened access and less trust between edges of networks, general lessening of the freeflow of data. This is where we are headed near term.

But there is also a version of this where you have social media platforms cultivating ways of influence that are utterly new, and incredibly dangerous for us. The reason for this is that statistically, masses of humans are predictable, and if anything is predictable, it can be modelled and steered whichever way one desires. Meta specifically already has a Swiss army knife set of labs and experiments regarding human attention, such as the brain lab, Meta glasses and many other projects, and TikToks algorithm is infamously designed to be addictive, which was a design that got copied over to other major content platforms such as Instagram and Youtube.

Another point to keep in mind is the soon-to-be explosion of personalised ads. Since humans and bots will be more clearly separable via traffic patterns, it becomes much easier to verify which traffic is human, and therefore which traffic should be targeted with ads. Given AIs general ability of synthesising scraps of information to get a good picture despite missing data, I believe ad targeting will become much more aggressive since the usual privacy preserving methods of restricting data you send and fragmenting your online identity can more easily be circumvented via AI analysis. Now of course this does not mean AI can identify you on the spot (although jailbroken Meta glasses can, which is another can of worms), but it does mean the typical safeguards became even thinner, without a clear supplement.

Current regulation targets the collection of data, while inferred data, which will become the key bridge that undercuts online privacy, is still in the grey area in most jurisdictions (for the EU, proving that inference occurred is the difficult part, let alone auditing it). Furthermore, unlike the dry reality of data collection, inferences tend to be mushy, dependent on the datasets they were trained on, and probabilistic, the last part being particularly troublesome for regulating. Since inference needs data, banning or severely restricting data collection practices further concedes any opportunity for a competitive European AI company, although given the current state of affairs, I am not sure there would have been one anyway (I do not consider Mistral competitive at this point in time given their model performance/cost ratios).

None of this is the exact dual internet that I sensed 10 months ago, and it will probably be messier and less boundaried than the concept is exhibited here, but I am confident there will be a further delineation between automated, AI-generated traffic (the botnet) and legitimate user traffic (the peoplenet), with new implications for internet privacy, the advertising industry and, given how much tech is embedded in our lives, our future.
